audience_note: Contains discussion of sexual coercion and exploitation of women by a military; researchers estimate hundreds of women were affected and describe many as abducted.

title: Women in the Korean War: volunteer corps and military comfort stations
summary: South Korea formally founded its Women's Army Corps on 6 September 1950, after leaders met in Pusan; many members broadcast appeals and propaganda to enemy troops from front-line positions. Separately, army documents show 'special comfort units' for soldiers in rear areas from about 1951 until March 1954, where women were held in conditions researchers describe as coerced.

uncertainty.note: WAC founded 1950; the comfort units have no clear start record and are estimated to 1951.

as_recorded.value: The Women's Army Corps was officially founded Sept 6, 1950
comfort station installation estimated at 1951; closed March 1954 (1954년 3월)

where.modern_name: Seoul, South Korea (also units at Gangneung, Chuncheon, Wonju and Sokcho)
where.historical_name: Seoul, Republic of Korea (wartime rear areas of the Korean peninsula)

importance.justification: Documents women's military service in the Korean War and the South Korean army's own comfort-station system, a subject acknowledged only decades later.

reviewer_note: Two distinct subjects joined in one record at the requester's instruction. Founding date 6 September 1950 comes from a 1960 Stars and Stripes piece. The comfort-unit facts (about 1951 start, closed March 1954, 89 women in 1952 per the army's 1956 Rear-Area Military History, an estimated 300 women in total by sociologist Kim Gwi-ok) come from a 2020 news report, not the army volume itself; the 1951 start is an estimate. The Women's Voluntary Labor Service Corps was not confirmed on an opened page and is not claimed.
